Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] mshta.exe HTA downloader reaching UAT-11795 staging domains (ClickFix) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — UAT-11795 deploys novel Starland RAT and bespoke WLDR C2 implant in financially
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanized software installer spawning embedded Python payload (Starland loader) · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Starland RAT / WLDR C2 beaconing to UAT-11795 HWID-parameterized domains · [LLM] Starland RAT blockchain fallback C2 via Polygon eth_call (polygon-rpc.com) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Telegram bot C2 / crypto-wallet exfiltration from script-host process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
mshta.exe HTA downloader reaching UAT-11795 staging domains (ClickFix) AIDelivery High
Hunts weaponized HTA execution via mshta.exe pulling remote HTAs from UAT-11795 staging infrastructure (eorthopaedics[.]com, zynaris[.]io, sastoro[.]com, web-devtools[.]com), the campaign's ClickFix-style initial access vector. Also flags mshta launched from a browser/explorer with a remote URL argument, the tell-tale shape of a copy-pasted ClickFix command. Rationale: Anchored on the four named staging domains (Talos: eorthopaedics[.]com/sastoro[.]com host the PS stage chain, zynaris[.]io hosts the ClickFix HTA, web-devtools[.]com serves shellcode) plus mshta remote-URL shape. Domains corroborated by the Cisco-Talos IOC repo and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://github.com/Cisco-Talos/IOCs/blob/main/2026/07/new-starland-rat-and-WLDR-implant-campaign.txt • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1566.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise app that legitimately launches signed .hta helpers from a whitelisted internal server (not these domains)
  • Legacy line-of-business tooling invoking mshta with a local http:// intranet URL
  • Security researcher/analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox VVM that reports to prod EDR
  • Web dev visiting web-devtools.com-looking legitimate portals — mitigated by requiring mshta as the process, not the browser
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any (".corp.",".local","intranet"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full mshta command line and the parent process. Confirm the URL host is one of the four staging domains and the .hta is remote, not a local intranet path. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block the staging domains at proxy/DNS, and kill the mshta and any child python.exe/PythonLauncher-* processes. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for trojanized installers (MobaXterm_v26.1.exe, WebEx_Client.exe, dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe, FaceitInstaller_x64.exe), outbound beacons to the C2 domains, and api.telegram.org / polygon-rpc.com callbacks.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("eorthopaedics.com","zynaris.io","sastoro.com","web-devtools.com")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://",".hta") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("eorthopaedics.com","zynaris.io","sastoro.com","web-devtools.com")
   or (CommandLine has_any ("http://","https://",".hta") and ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","explorer.exe"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized software installer spawning embedded Python payload (Starland loader) AIInstallation High
Detects UAT-11795 trojanized installers (MobaXterm_v26.1.exe, WebEx_Client.exe, dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe, FaceitInstaller_x64.exe) executing their NSIS-bundled byte-compiled Python loader — spawning python.exe/pythonw.exe or a PythonLauncher-{3char} process that decodes and runs Starland RAT in memory. Article-specific supply-chain/user-execution pivot. Rationale: Uses the four exact trojanized filenames from Talos Table 1 as the parent, and the code-block string 'PythonLauncher-{3 random characters}' plus python.exe as the byte-compiled loader child. Very low FP because legit MobaXterm/WebEx/DBeaver/FACEIT installers do not spawn Python. Filenames corroborated by SecurityAffairs and the Talos IOC repo. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195532/malware/new-russian-campaign-uses-fake-webex-and-zoom-installers-to-deploy-starland-rat.html • https://github.com/Cisco-Talos/IOCs/blob/main/2026/07/new-starland-rat-and-WLDR-implant-campaign.txt
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.006 T1027.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine but coincidentally similarly-named repackaged installer in a software-deployment lab
  • DBeaver CE genuinely bundling a Python-based plugin runtime (rare; the CE installer name here is the trojan's exact filename)
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample generating EDR telemetry into prod
  • Internal app-packaging team testing NSIS wrappers that shell out to python.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\SoftwareRepackaging\\","\\PackagingLab\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the parent installer (SHA256) and compare against the Talos IOC bundle; confirm it dropped/launched python from a temp or install dir. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the installer and the PythonLauncher-* binary, and terminate the python process tree. 3) Hunt: check for the download URL the installer came from (web-devtools.com / zynaris.io), Starland C2 beacons, and Telegram execution beacons to bots 8384531459 / 7993597060.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MobaXterm_v26.1.exe","WebEx_Client.exe","dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe","FaceitInstaller_x64.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe") or FileName matches regex @"(?i)PythonLauncher-[A-Za-z0-9]{3}" or ProcessCommandLine has "PythonLauncher-"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("MobaXterm_v26.1.exe","WebEx_Client.exe","dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe","FaceitInstaller_x64.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pythonw.exe" or CommandLine has "PythonLauncher-"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Starland RAT / WLDR C2 beaconing to UAT-11795 HWID-parameterized domains AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound connections or DNS to UAT-11795 C2/staging domains (eorthopaedics[.]com, sastoro[.]com, windowscreenrepairnearme[.]com, aipythondevs[.]com, web-devtools[.]com), which carry HWID-parameterized paths (/feed/, /alpha/) for per-victim Starland RAT and WLDR agent C2. Domain IOCs are high-fidelity and second-source confirmed. Rationale: All five domains are named Talos IOCs (eorthopaedics/sastoro = /feed/ & /alpha/ HWID C2 for WLDR; windowscreenrepairnearme/aipythondevs = Starland RAT C2; web-devtools = shellcode staging). Confirmed by the Cisco-Talos IOC repo and BleepingComputer. Domain match alone is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://github.com/Cisco-Talos/IOCs/blob/main/2026/07/new-starland-rat-and-WLDR-implant-campaign.txt • https://gbhackers.com/starland-rat-steals-browser-credentials/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1132.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • eorthopaedics[.]com and windowscreenrepairnearme[.]com are likely hijacked legitimate domains — a genuine patient/customer visiting the real site could resolve it (mitigate by requiring the /feed/ or /alpha/ HWID path or a script-host process)
  • Threat-intel enrichment tools or sandbox VMs resolving the IOCs for research
  • URL-scanning security proxies pre-fetching the domains
  • Passive DNS / TI feed replication traffic on a sensor host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process that initiated the connection (Defender/Falcon carry ContextImageFileName); a python/PythonLauncher/powershell client to these domains is a confirmed beacon. Check the URL path for the volume-serial HWID and /feed/ or /alpha/. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the domains at DNS+proxy, isolate the host, capture memory (Starland/WLDR are in-memory). 3) Hunt: pivot on the HWID to find sibling infections, check for CastleStealer/Remcos second-stage, polygon-rpc.com fallback, and Telegram beacons.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

Starland RAT blockchain fallback C2 via Polygon eth_call (polygon-rpc.com) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the Starland RAT fallback C2 resolution: a script-host process (python/PythonLauncher/powershell) making a JSON-RPC eth_call to polygon-rpc.com to read an XOR-encrypted fallback domain from Polygon contract 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba. A non-crypto endpoint talking to a public Ethereum RPC via a scripting interpreter is a strong, article-specific anomaly. Rationale: External search corroboration identified the exact fallback path: eth_call to polygon-rpc.com against contract 0x6ae382ed... (selector 0xc659f3b8, XOR key $m7*rYpry3). Requiring a script-host process (not a browser/wallet app) reaching a public Ethereum RPC keeps FP manageable. Enriched from GBHackers and the Talos blog. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://gbhackers.com/starland-rat-steals-browser-credentials/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195532/malware/new-russian-campaign-uses-fake-webex-and-zoom-installers-to-deploy-starland-rat.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web3/blockchain developer running Python (web3.py) or PowerShell scripts against polygon-rpc.com
  • Crypto trading bots or node-monitoring scripts on a dev workstation
  • DeFi/NFT tooling that legitimately batches eth_call requests
  • Security researcher reproducing the fallback resolution in a lab (note the Sentinel/Splunk DNS-only variants lack process context and are hunting-grade)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("web3","ethers","hardhat","truffle","brownie")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating binary is python/PythonLauncher/powershell (not a browser or a known wallet). Capture the raw JSON-RPC body if proxy logs exist and check for method eth_call + contract 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba / selector 0xc659f3b8. 2) Contain: isolate host, block polygon-rpc.com egress for non-approved hosts, memory-capture the interpreter. 3) Hunt: XOR-decrypt (key $m7*rYpry3) is done in-memory — pivot to the resolved fallback domain in DNS logs and correlate with the primary C2 domains and Telegram beacons.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "polygon-rpc.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)PythonLauncher-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "polygon-rpc.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Telegram bot C2 / crypto-wallet exfiltration from script-host process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects UAT-11795 execution/exfiltration beacons to api.telegram.org (bots 8384531459 'skuefq_bot' and 7993597060 'komandastuk_bot') that carry victim machine fingerprints and cryptocurrency-wallet inventories. Scoped to script-host initiating processes to separate malware beacons from legitimate Telegram Desktop usage. Rationale: Article names two actor Telegram bots (8384531459 skuefq_bot, 7993597060 komandastuk_bot) receiving HWID fingerprints and wallet inventories. Bot tokens live only in-memory, so the reliable network anchor is api.telegram.org from a non-Telegram-client script host. Corroborated by GBHackers (40+ wallet scan) and SecurityAffairs. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://gbhackers.com/starland-rat-steals-browser-credentials/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195532/malware/new-russian-campaign-uses-fake-webex-and-zoom-installers-to-deploy-starland-rat.html
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1102.002 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PowerShell/Python DevOps scripts that send alerts via a corporate Telegram bot
  • CI/CD or monitoring automation posting to Telegram from a build host
  • A developer testing the Telegram Bot API locally with python-telegram-bot
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample (note DNS-only Sentinel/Splunk variants are hunting-grade — no process context)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("\\ci\\","\\jenkins\\","alerting","monitoring","notify")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is a script host, not Telegram Desktop; if proxy/TLS-inspection is available, check the URI for /bot8384531459: or /bot7993597060: and sendMessage/sendDocument. 2) Contain: isolate host, revoke exposed browser/wallet credentials, block api.telegram.org for non-sanctioned hosts. 3) Hunt: correlate with wallet-file/browser-credential reads on the same host, the Starland/WLDR C2 domains, and installer origin; treat any exfiltrated wallet as compromised and rotate.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)PythonLauncher-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "api.telegram.org"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: UAT-11795 Telegram Bot C2 Beacon from Script Host
id: b2c3d4e5-7f80-4911-9b2c-4d6e8f0a2b35
description: Detects a scripting interpreter beaconing to api.telegram.org, matching UAT-11795 Telegram bot C2/exfil.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/30
tags:
  - attack.t1102.002
  - attack.t1041
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Initiated: 'true'
    DestinationHostname|contains: 'api.telegram.org'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:*api.telegram.org* (@Image:(*\python.exe OR *\pythonw.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\mshta.exe))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/api\.telegram\.org$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(pythonw?|powershell|pwsh|mshta)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="*api.telegram.org" by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="*api.telegram.org" by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,

let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["eorthopaedics.com", "sastoro.com", "web-devtools.com", "zynaris.io", "windowscreenrepairnearme.com", "aipythondevs.com"]);
ImNetworkSession

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental

    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /

    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

title: Scheduled Task Creation with Suspicious Image / Encoded Args
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0d
status: experimental
description: |
    schtasks.exe /create with payload-shaped action — points at
    powershell, cmd, rundll32, encoded-base64, or user-writable paths.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1053.005
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_schtasks:
        Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: '/create'
    selection_payload:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'powershell'
            - 'cmd.exe'
            - 'rundll32'
            - '-enc'
            - 'FromBase64'
            - '\Users\Public'
            - '\AppData\'
    condition: selection_schtasks and selection_payload
falsepositives:
    - GPO-driven scheduled tasks, MDT/SCCM imaging
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious @velora-dex/sdk (9.4.1/9.4.2) pulled into GitHub Actions build runner
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] npm/node install-time payload: package manager spawning curl/launchctl/osascript on a runner · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Velora macOS backdoor launchctl persistence (com.apple.Terminal.profiler.plist) · [LLM] Shai-Hulud worm artifacts written on GitHub Actions runner (shai-hulud-workflow.yml / bundle.js) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Build runner beacon/exfil to Velora backdoor C2 (89.36.224.5 / datahub.ink) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Malicious @velora-dex/sdk (9.4.1/9.4.2) pulled into GitHub Actions build runner AIDelivery High
Hunts CI/build runners that install the trojanized @velora-dex/sdk npm package — the compromise that dropped a macOS backdoor the moment the SDK was imported. Version 9.4.0 is confirmed clean, so any install of a non-9.4.0 version of this specific package on a runner is suspect. Rationale: Anchors on the exact compromised package name '@velora-dex/sdk' and excludes the confirmed-clean 9.4.0, per Corgea (v9.4.1 published 2026-04-07) and StepSecurity — a named-package/version IOC that only fires on genuinely-affected installs. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence • https://github.com/VeloraDEX/sdk/issues/233
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer intentionally installing the clean 9.4.0 pin (excluded, but a lockfile resolving without an explicit version tag may show no version)
  • Internal mirror/registry proxy re-fetching the package name in log lines during cache warmup
  • Security researchers/DFIR reproducing the compromise in a sandbox runner
  • A vendored monorepo referencing 'velora-dex/sdk' in a path or comment picked up by broad command lines
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk@9.4.0") | where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the exact resolved version from the runner's package-lock.json/npm cache and the workflow run; 9.4.1/9.4.2 = confirmed malicious, 9.4.0 = clean. 2) Contain: isolate the runner (especially macOS/Bitrise hosts), revoke any secrets that were in scope for that job (Apple signing certs, App Store Connect keys, registry/deploy tokens), and rebuild the runner from a clean image. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'C2 beacon to Velora infra (89.36.224.5)' and the launchctl-persistence UC on the same DeviceId, and diff lockfiles across all repos for the pinned bad version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk"
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk@9.4.0" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk@9.4.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk"
| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk@9.4.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Build runner beacon/exfil to Velora backdoor C2 (89.36.224.5 / datahub.ink) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any outbound connection from a runner or endpoint to the confirmed Velora-SDK backdoor C2 infrastructure — IP 89.36.224.5 and domains datahub.ink, cloud-sync.online, byte-io.us. These are where the macOS implant fetched its shell script and exfiltrated harvested signing keys and tokens. Rationale: IP 89.36.224.5 is confirmed as the Velora backdoor C2 by StepSecurity, Corgea and Phoenix Security; the three domains are enumerated verbatim in Corgea's IOC list. Direct-hit IOC match, near-zero legitimate reason for a build host to reach these. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://phoenix.security/velora-dex-sdk-supply-chain-compromise-build-pipeline-injection-delivers-macos-persistent-implant/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox tooling actively probing the C2 (verify the initiating process is a scanner)
  • A newly-registered legitimate service reusing the 89.36.224.5 host after takedown (re-validate IP ownership)
  • Security team detonating the sample in an authorized lab connected to production telemetry
  • DNS sinkhole or passive-DNS collector resolving the domains for research
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("threatintel-scanner.exe","nessus","nmap")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the runner (node/npm/curl vs a legit tool) and the direction/volume of traffic to 89.36.224.5. 2) Contain: block the IP and three domains at egress/proxy, isolate the host, and immediately rotate every secret the affected build job could touch (Apple signing certs, provisioning profiles, App Store Connect keys, registry tokens). 3) Hunt: correlate against the @velora-dex/sdk install UC and the launchctl-persistence UC on the same host, and search all runners for prior connections to these indicators.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "89.36.224.5"
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("datahub.ink","cloud-sync.online","byte-io.us")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr == "89.36.224.5" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = DstIpAddr, Detail = Url),
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has_any ("datahub.ink","cloud-sync.online","byte-io.us") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = DnsQuery, Detail = DnsResponseName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Velora macOS backdoor launchctl persistence (com.apple.Terminal.profiler.plist) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the persistence artifacts the Velora SDK backdoor installs on macOS build runners: a masquerading LaunchAgent plist and support directory impersonating Apple's Terminal, plus the known payload hashes. Fires on the exact plist name, path, or file hash written to a runner. Rationale: com.apple.Terminal.profiler.plist and the ~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.Terminal/profiler directory are the exact persistence artifacts documented by Corgea; the plist name masquerades as Apple's Terminal but is not a genuine Apple file, so any write is high-fidelity. Payload SHA256s are the article-supplied IOCs, kept alongside the corroborated path artifacts. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://opensourcemalware.com/blog/velora-hacked • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Apple/Terminal update writing legitimately-named plists (the profiler variant is not a real Apple file, so overlap is unlikely)
  • EDR/DFIR tooling restoring a quarantined sample onto a lab host
  • Backup/restore software rehydrating a previously-infected user Library
  • Analyst manually copying the IOC file for reverse-engineering on a monitored host
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged macOS runner, confirm the plist exists under ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ and check `launchctl list` for the zsh.profiler service and the com.apple.Terminal/profiler support dir. 2) Contain: unload the LaunchAgent (launchctl bootout / remove plist), kill the profiler binary, isolate the host, and rotate all Apple signing material and CI secrets that lived on it. 3) Hunt: pivot to the 89.36.224.5 C2 UC and the @velora-dex/sdk install UC on the same DeviceId, and sweep the macOS fleet for the plist name and payload hashes.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" and FileName =~ "com.apple.Terminal.profiler.plist")
   or FolderPath has "com.apple.Terminal/profiler"
   or SHA256 in ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270","0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "com.apple.Terminal.profiler.plist" and TargetFilePath has "/LaunchAgents/")
   or TargetFilePath has "com.apple.Terminal/profiler"
   or TargetFileSHA256 in ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270","0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm/node install-time payload: package manager spawning curl/launchctl/osascript on a runner AIExploitation Medium
Behavioural catch for the Velora-class TTP where importing a poisoned npm package makes node call child_process.exec() to download and persist a payload. Surfaces node/npm/yarn/pnpm/bun spawning curl, wget, osascript, chmod or launchctl during a build — catching variants and future-versioned repackages the static IOCs miss. Rationale: Models the corroborated execution mechanism (dist/index.js calling child_process.exec() to curl a shell script then launchctl-persist) as a parent/child pivot, so it catches the campaign's behaviour beyond the pinned version/IOCs. Kept as hunting because legit postinstall scripts also spawn curl. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://phoenix.security/velora-dex-sdk-supply-chain-compromise-build-pipeline-injection-delivers-macos-persistent-implant/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate npm postinstall scripts (node-sass, node-gyp, puppeteer, esbuild) that curl/wget a prebuilt binary
  • Build scripts that chmod +x downloaded CLI tools
  • macOS packaging steps invoking osascript for notarization/UI prompts
  • Corporate proxy bootstrap scripts run under node during CI setup
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","github.com","githubusercontent.com","nodejs.org"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command line — a curl/wget to an unfamiliar host, a launchctl load of an unknown plist, or chmod +x on a freshly-downloaded file is malicious; a fetch to a known package CDN (github.com, npmjs.org) is likely benign. 2) Contain: if the destination or plist is unrecognised, isolate the runner and rotate its secrets. 3) Hunt: pivot on the downloaded host/IP against the C2 UC (89.36.224.5) and check for the launchctl-persistence plist on the same host; diff the repo lockfile for newly-added dependencies.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","yarn","pnpm","bun")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","osascript","launchctl","chmod")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm","yarn","pnpm","bun")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","osascript","launchctl","chmod")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud worm artifacts written on GitHub Actions runner (shai-hulud-workflow.yml / bundle.js) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the self-replicating Shai-Hulud npm worm's on-disk artifacts as they appear on a compromised runner: the shai-hulud-workflow.yml propagation workflow and the known malicious bundle.js payload hash. Distinct filesystem pivot from the Velora backdoor detections. Rationale: shai-hulud-workflow.yml is the worm's signature propagation artifact and 46faab8ab153...628f09 is the documented malicious bundle.js SHA-256, both corroborated by Unit42, Wiz and Datadog Security Labs — filesystem IOCs with no legitimate reason to exist on a runner. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher intentionally checking out an infected repo to a monitored host for analysis
  • IOC-sweep tooling writing sample copies of shai-hulud-workflow.yml to disk during hunting
  • A defensive canary/honeypot repo deliberately seeded with the artifact name
  • Backup restoration of a previously-infected repository working tree
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path/hash on the runner and identify the initiating process and the repo/workflow it landed in; a true hit means the worm executed and likely harvested tokens. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, revoke npm publish tokens and GitHub PATs the job held, and remove any pushed 'shai-hulud' branch / shai-hulud-workflow.yml from affected repos before it self-propagates. 3) Hunt: enumerate packages published by the compromised token, search for repos with the description marker 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming', and sweep all runners for the workflow filename and bundle.js hash.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "shai-hulud-workflow.yml"
   or SHA256 == "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "shai-hulud-workflow.yml"
   or TargetFileSHA256 =~ "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d") or SHA1 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d") or MD5 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d") or SHA1 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d") or MD5 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Harden-Runner Block Mode Now Available for macOS and Windows GitHub-Hosted Runners

StepSecurity
2026-07-16 6 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Harden-Runner v2.20.0 extends egress block mode to macOS and Windows GitHub-hosted runners, so you can stop secret exfiltration on every OS your pipelines run on, not just observe it.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised @velora-dex/sdk npm package (9.4.1/9.4.2) installed on CI runner
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] MiniRAT launchctl persistence established during macOS CI build
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] CI runner egress to MiniRAT C2 89.36.224.5 (Velora SDK backdoor) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] CI runner egress to Megalodon secret-exfil C2 216.126.225.129:8443
Compromised @velora-dex/sdk npm package (9.4.1/9.4.2) installed on CI runner AIDelivery High
Hunts for the known-trojanized @velora-dex/sdk package landing in node_modules on a macOS/Windows/Linux build runner. Version 9.4.1 injected a base64 loader into dist/index.js that fires on import and pulls a macOS Go RAT (MiniRAT); 9.4.2 was the hurried revert — presence of either on a runner warrants review. Rationale: Anchors on the exact compromised package path '@velora-dex/sdk' confirmed by Corgea, safedep and StepSecurity; on an ephemeral CI runner any occurrence of this known-bad dependency is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://safedep.io/malicious-velora-dex-sdk-npm-compromised-rat/ • https://github.com/VeloraDEX/sdk/issues/233
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or internal IR team detonating the sample in a sandbox that is also EDR-monitored
  • A pinned lockfile deliberately holding 9.4.2 (reverted) for regression testing
  • Mirror/proxy cache warming that pre-fetches many package versions including these
  • A developer reproducing the advisory locally to confirm exposure
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cape.exe","procmon.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the repo/workflow that pulled @velora-dex/sdk and the exact version from the lockfile; check the runner's outbound connections to 89.36.224.5 in the same job window. 2) Contain: fail/cancel the pipeline, rotate every secret the job could touch (Apple signing certs, App Store Connect keys, Windows code-signing certs, OIDC/cloud tokens), and pin the dependency to a known-good pre-9.4.1 version or the vendor-verified fix. 3) Hunt: sweep all runners and developer macOS hosts for MiniRAT launchctl persistence and for egress to 89.36.224.5 / 216.126.225.129.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "@velora-dex/sdk" or FolderPath has @"@velora-dex\sdk"
| where FileName endswith ".js" or FileName =~ "package.json"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "@velora-dex/sdk" or TargetFilePath has "@velora-dex\\sdk"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CI runner egress to MiniRAT C2 89.36.224.5 (Velora SDK backdoor) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any outbound connection from a runner or build host to 89.36.224.5, the C2 that the injected @velora-dex/sdk loader contacts to fetch its architecture-specific macOS shell-script/Go RAT stager. A hard IOC — no legitimate build should reach this host. Rationale: 89.36.224.5 is the confirmed MiniRAT stager/C2 host (Corgea, safedep) referenced by the article's Velora SDK compromise; a single hard-IOC destination match needs no behavioural qualifier. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://safedep.io/malicious-velora-dex-sdk-npm-compromised-rat/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/scanning service that actively probes known C2 IPs from a monitored host
  • IR sandbox detonation of the sample with live network
  • Security team reproducing the advisory to validate blast radius
  • Shared NAT egress where a non-runner host on the same egress IP is the real source (verify DeviceName/src)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process (expect node/npm-spawned sh/curl) and whether @velora-dex/sdk is in the job's dependency tree. 2) Contain: block 89.36.224.5 at egress/firewall, isolate the runner/host, and rotate all secrets the pipeline exposed. 3) Hunt: pivot to launchctl persistence (MiniRAT) and to Megalodon C2 216.126.225.129:8443 across the fleet; review recent installs of @velora-dex/sdk org-wide.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "89.36.224.5"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "89.36.224.5"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CI runner egress to Megalodon secret-exfil C2 216.126.225.129:8443 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects outbound connections to 216.126.225.129 (notably TCP 8443), the confirmed Megalodon C2 that received compressed archives of harvested CI secrets, cloud creds, SSH keys and OIDC tokens via HTTPS POST across 5,500+ repos. Any runner reaching this host indicates active secret exfiltration. Rationale: 216.126.225.129:8443 is the corroborated Megalodon HTTPS-POST exfil C2 (StepSecurity, safedep, Phoenix); a destination-IP match is a hard IOC requiring no behavioural context. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/megalodon-mass-github-actions-secret-exfiltration-across-5-500-public-repositories • https://safedep.io/megalodon-mass-github-repo-backdooring-ci-workflows/ • https://phoenix.security/megalodon-ci-github-actions-workflow-poisoning-credential-harvesting/
ATT&CKT1041 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TI enrichment scanner probing the known C2 from a monitored host
  • IR sandbox detonation with live egress
  • Shared-egress NAT attributing another host's traffic to a runner (validate src/DeviceName)
  • Deliberate purple-team replay of the Megalodon workflow payload
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the runner/repo and confirm whether an injected workflow (e.g. SysDiag / Optimize-Build, forged authors build-bot/auto-ci/ci-bot/pipeline-bot) or malicious dependency initiated the connection; capture bytes sent. 2) Contain: block 216.126.225.129, cancel the pipeline, and treat every secret reachable by that job as compromised — rotate immediately. 3) Hunt: review GitHub Actions workflow files for base64 bash payloads POSTing to :8443, enumerate other repos with the same injected workflow, and correlate with @velora-dex/sdk installs and 89.36.224.5 egress.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteIP == "216.126.225.129"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "216.126.225.129"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetworkBytes, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MiniRAT launchctl persistence established during macOS CI build AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for launchctl registering a LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon during a build, spawned from a shell/node/curl parent — the persistence step MiniRAT uses after the @velora-dex/sdk loader drops its arch-specific Go binary. Ephemeral GitHub-hosted macOS runners should never establish OS-level persistence mid-job. Rationale: Maps the MiniRAT launchctl-persistence step (StepSecurity/iru) to the parent chain (node-spawned shell → launchctl load) that a stager uses; on ephemeral runners any mid-build persistence is inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence • https://www.iru.com/blog/minirat • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1543.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Xcode/fastlane or Homebrew setup steps that legitimately load helper LaunchAgents during app-signing jobs
  • Self-hosted macOS runner bootstrap scripts registering the runner service via launchctl
  • Rosetta/simulator tooling loading daemons on first run
  • Developer macOS host installing a legitimate background service via a shell installer
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "actions.runner" and ProcessCommandLine !has "com.github.actions" and ProcessCommandLine !has "fastlane"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the launchctl target plist path and the referenced program binary; confirm the grandparent traces to node/npm and whether @velora-dex/sdk is present or 89.36.224.5 was contacted. 2) Contain: kill the persistence item (launchctl bootout / unload), quarantine the dropped binary, isolate the host, and rotate signing certs/keys handled by that runner. 3) Hunt: search DeviceFileEvents for plist writes to ~/Library/LaunchAgents or /Library/LaunchDaemons during builds and pivot to the two campaign C2 IPs across all macOS hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "launchctl"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("load","bootstrap","submit")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","node","curl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "launchctl"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("load","bootstrap","submit")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","zsh","node","curl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Coordinated AsyncAPI Supply Chain Attack: Miasma RAT Delivered via Compromised CI/CD Pipelines in Two Repositories

StepSecurity
2026-07-16 15 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 14, 2026 at 07:10 UTC, three packages in the AsyncAPI generator monorepo (@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, @asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1, and @asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1) were published to npm carrying an obfuscated dropper that fires the moment the library is loaded, not on install. The packages were published through the project's own legitimate GitHub Actions release workflow and carry valid npm OIDC provenance attestations, because the attacker didn't steal an npm token: they gained push access to the repository's next branch and let the project's real CI/CD pipeline do the …

Miasma RAT C2 beacon to 85.137.53.71 from Node.js runtime AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the StepSecurity/Harden-Runner-confirmed Miasma HTTP C2 endpoint 85.137.53.71 (three ports) originating from a Node.js process after a compromised @asyncapi package is loaded. Article-specific because the dropper fires on library load and beacons to this exact confirmed IP. Rationale: 85.137.53.71 is StepSecurity/Harden-Runner-confirmed (observed egress directly) and cross-verified by Socket.dev and Safedep as the Miasma HTTP C2 on three ports; any host contacting it is a confirmed compromise. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/miasma-worm-returns-to-npm/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer VPN/proxy egressing through an IP that happens to overlap after reassignment (verify WHOIS ownership before closing)
  • Threat-intel sandbox or research VM intentionally detonating the sample
  • Security scanner validating IOC reachability from a jump host
  • Shared NAT gateway masking which internal host actually beaconed
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal src host and the initiating process (expect node.exe); pull the full process tree and the loaded @asyncapi package version. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 85.137.53.71 at egress on all three ports, and kill the node process; rotate any developer secrets on that host (npm/GitHub/AWS tokens, SSH keys) as Miasma is a credential stealer. 3) Hunt: sweep for other hosts contacting 85.137.53.71 or resolving the fallback channels, and inventory all machines with the malicious @asyncapi versions installed.

| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession

| where DstIpAddr == "85.137.53.71"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js resolving Miasma fallback C2 channels (BitTorrent DHT / Nostr relays) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS resolution / connections from a Node.js process to Miasma's fallback dead-drop resolver infrastructure — router.bittorrent.com, dht.transmissionbt.com, relay.damus.io, relay.nostr.com — used when the primary HTTP C2 is unavailable. Legit Node apps almost never touch BitTorrent DHT bootstrap or Nostr relays. Rationale: Harden-Runner directly observed router.bittorrent.com and dht.transmissionbt.com egress; Socket.dev and Safedep confirm Nostr relays (relay.damus.io/relay.nostr.com) and BitTorrent DHT as documented Miasma fallback channels — a Node.js process touching these is high-signal. Detached 'node -e' launcher downloading Miasma second stage from IPFS AIInstallation High
Hunts the Miasma launcher pattern: a Node.js process spawning a hidden/detached child 'node -e' that pulls sync.js from an IPFS gateway. The command line carries IPFS/sync.js/NodeJS markers, distinguishing it from benign node -e build helpers. Rationale: Socket.dev and Safedep both document the launcher spawning a detached 'node -e' child that downloads sync.js from an IPFS gateway into a hidden NodeJS directory; node-parenting-node with -e plus IPFS/sync.js markers is the article-specific execution fingerprint. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build tooling that legitimately shells out to node -e for a quick eval (e.g. version print)
  • A developer manually using an IPFS Node library (js-ipfs / helia) for legitimate work
  • Electron/desktop apps that self-spawn node -e helper processes
  • Postinstall scripts of unrelated packages invoking node -e
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("console.log(process.version)","--version") and ProcessCommandLine !has "ipfs")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full -e payload string and decode the IPFS CID/gateway URL; confirm the parent is a build/CI or dev-tool node process loading @asyncapi. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill both node processes, remove the dropped NodeJS\sync.js, and block the C2/fallback infra; rotate secrets on the host. 3) Hunt: search for the same node->node -e chain org-wide and for sync.js drops (see companion file-drop UC).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-e"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ipfs","sync.js","NodeJS")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-e"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ipfs","sync.js","NodeJS")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma sync.js payload dropped to hidden 'NodeJS' directory AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the second-stage write: sync.js landing in the OS-specific hidden 'NodeJS' directory under a user profile, or a file matching the known Miasma dropper hashes. This is the on-disk staging step the launcher performs before spawning the detached RAT. Rationale: All four write-ups (StepSecurity, Socket.dev, Safedep, JFrog) describe the payload dropping sync.js into an OS-specific hidden 'NodeJS' directory; the filename+path and the article's three SHA256 dropper hashes make this a precise on-disk anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://research.jfrog.com/post/miasma-worm-returns-to-npm/
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate app that happens to create a user-profile 'NodeJS' folder with an unrelated sync.js (rare)
  • Corporate software distributing a signed sync.js helper
  • Backup/EDR agents touching the file during scan (initiating process would not be node.exe)
  • Developer manually placing a sync.js script in a NodeJS-named workspace
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node") or isnotempty(SHA256)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is node.exe and hash the dropped sync.js against the three known IOCs; determine which @asyncapi package triggered it. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine/delete NodeJS\sync.js, kill the detached node process, and rotate developer secrets. 3) Hunt: submit the sample hash to the fleet, sweep all hosts for the hidden NodeJS\sync.js path, and correlate with C2 beacons to 85.137.53.71.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "sync.js" and TargetFilePath has "NodeJS")

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Installation of compromised @asyncapi package versions AIDelivery Medium
Hunts install/CI commands that pull the exact malicious @asyncapi versions (generator@3.3.1, generator-helpers@1.1.1, generator-components@0.7.1, specs@6.11.2). Detects the supply-chain initial-access moment when a build agent or developer ingests the trojanized packages. Rationale: The affected-versions table names the exact malicious releases (last-safe 3.3.0/1.1.0/0.7.0/6.11.1); Socket.dev confirms all five versions were published and later unpublished, so any install command pinning these exact versions ingested the Miasma dropper. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A researcher or IR team intentionally reproducing the compromise in a sandbox
  • Internal mirror/cache scan enumerating package names (not an actual install)
  • A pinned reference in documentation/ticket text captured by a shell (no real fetch)
  • Security tooling querying npm for the version to check exposure
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the command actually installed (vs. referenced) the version and identify the host/build agent and whether the library was subsequently loaded (node process launch). 2) Contain: remove the malicious versions, pin to last-safe (3.3.0/1.1.0/0.7.0/6.11.1), purge node_modules and caches, and rotate all developer/CI secrets since Miasma harvests npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH credentials. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host and CI runner with these versions, then correlate with the C2 (85.137.53.71), sync.js drop, and node -e launcher detections.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc

| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]","@asyncapi/[email protected]")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
