First-seen SOAP client on MantisBT mantisconnect.php (new source, post-bypass admin activity) AIExploitation Medium
Baseline anti-join surfacing source IPs that hit /api/soap/mantisconnect.php for the first time in 30 days — the shape of an attacker abusing the CVE-2026-47156 bypass to act with administrator privileges from a source that was never a legitimate SOAP integration. Prioritises new clients returning HTTP 200 with large payloads. Rationale: SOAP integrations are stable, allow-listable source IPs; a never-before-seen IP driving mantisconnect.php POSTs is the cleanest available proxy for post-bypass privileged abuse when request bodies aren't logged. Leftanti/append baseline anti-join is a distinct pivot from UC1 (correlation) and UC2 (threshold). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-47156/ • https://mantisbt.org/docs/master-1.3.x/en-US/Admin_Guide/html/admin.config.soap.html
ATT&CKT1550.004 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.All_Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A newly-deployed or relocated legitimate SOAP integration (new server, new egress IP after cloud migration)
  • Occasional developer testing the SOAP API from a workstation
  • DHCP/NAT change putting an existing integration behind a different public IP
  • Vulnerability scanner probing the SOAP endpoint for the first time this month
Suppression filter
| where src NOT IN [| inputlookup mantis_soap_allowlist.csv | fields src] // maintain an allowlist of sanctioned SOAP integration source IPs to suppress known-good new-but-authorized clients
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the new source IP (ASN/geo/reverse DNS) and compare its User-Agent to known integrations; confirm POSTs returned 200 with non-trivial bytes. 2) Contain: if unrecognised, block at the WAF and disable any account seen authenticating from it; rotate the admin cookie_string. 3) Hunt: 30-day baseline warms this rule — during warmup, manually validate each new IP against the sanctioned-integration inventory and pivot into UC2 (volume) and UC1 (signup) for the same IP to confirm the full CVE-2026-47156 chain.
let baseline = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))

| order by BytesOut desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:

            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'

            - '\brave.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high

1) Triage: identify the source device and the process that opened the socket (InitiatingProcessFileName/ContextImageFileName); confirm it is an IoT/Linux asset and whether the connection succeeded. 2) Contain: block 209.182.237.133, 185.10.68.127 and *.digikalas.online at the firewall/DNS, isolate the device from the LAN, and preserve the running binary. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same src for Telnet/ADB scanner fan-out (UC2), DNS to digikalas.online subdomains and TXT queries (UC3), and search the fleet for the SHA256 71dfbb17… (UC4).

| where RemoteIP in (c2ips) or RemoteUrl has "digikalas.online"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

TuxBot Telnet/ADB scanner fan-out (credential brute-force propagation) AIDelivery Medium
Detects a single host spraying outbound connections to many public destinations on the Telnet (23/2323) and Android Debug Bridge (5555) ports — the working infection vector of TuxBot's Telnet scanner (1,496 credential pairs) and ADB scanner. High-fidelity because near-zero legitimate endpoints fan out across these IoT-specific ports. Rationale: Targets TuxBot's confirmed working infection vector — the Telnet scanner (1,496 cred pairs) plus ADB (5555) scanner — via a fan-out threshold on the exact scanner ports; ports 23/2323/5555 have essentially no benign endpoint fan-out, making the volume signal high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-tuxbot-v3-iot-botnet-uses-llm-generated-code/
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Rumble) sweeping the estate on Telnet/ADB ports
  • Shodan-style internet-wide research scanner running from a sanctioned host
  • Network/asset-discovery tool enumerating IoT/OT gear on 23/2323
  • Mobile-device test lab legitimately probing ADB 5555 across many devices
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.20.0.5","10.20.0.6")   // approved vuln-scanner source IPs — replace with your scanner allowlist
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source is not a sanctioned scanner (check asset inventory / scanner allowlist) and review the initiating process and destination geo-spread. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network and block egress on 23/2323/5555; if it is an unmanaged IoT device, quarantine its switch port/VLAN. 3) Hunt: check the same host for C2 to the UC1 IPs/domain and for the SHA256 71dfbb… (UC4); pull authentication logs on any internal targets it reached on port 23 for successful weak-credential logons.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","ConnectionFailed")
| where RemotePort in (23, 2323, 5555)   // Telnet, alt-Telnet, Android Debug Bridge scanners
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP), Ports = make_set(RemotePort), Attempts = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where DistinctTargets > 100   // botnet scanner sprays thousands; >100 distinct public IoT ports/day is abnormal for one endpoint
| order by DistinctTargets desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort in (23, 2323, 5555)
| where ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) == false
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort), Attempts = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DeviceVendor
| where DistinctTargets > 100   // fan-out threshold for IoT scanner behaviour
| order by DistinctTargets desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=23 OR RemotePort=2323 OR RemotePort=5555)
| cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4, negate=true)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=DistinctTargets))
| DistinctTargets > 100
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true dc(All_Traffic.dest) as distinct_targets count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (23,2323,5555) by All_Traffic.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where distinct_targets > 100
| sort - distinct_targets
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest) as distinct_targets count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (23,2323,5555) by All_Traffic.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where distinct_targets > 100
| sort - distinct_targets
TuxBot fallback C2 via digikalas.online DGA subdomains and DNS TXT queries AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts TuxBot's fall-back C2 channels: DNS lookups to the developer domain digikalas.online (and algorithmically-generated subdomains like newtuxdev.sevielw.digikalas.online) and DNS TXT queries used as a covert command channel. Article-specific because digikalas.online is the confirmed live operator domain and DNS TXT / SHA512-DGA are named fall-back mechanisms. Rationale: Keys on the confirmed live operator domain digikalas.online (resolving on Arvan Cloud) and the named SHA512-DGA / DNS-TXT fall-back channels; the leaked subdomain newtuxdev.sevielw.digikalas.online proves the actor uses multi-label subdomains under this parent, so any resolution is high-value. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://securityonline.info/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1568.002 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign DNS TXT lookups for SPF/DKIM/DMARC verification by mail servers and security tools
  • Domain-monitoring/threat-intel platforms actively resolving digikalas.online for tracking
  • Certificate/ACME validation issuing TXT queries at scale
  • Passive-DNS or brand-protection crawlers enumerating the parent domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("named","dnsmasq","systemd-resolved") and RemoteUrl endswith "digikalas.online"
Response runbook
1) Triage: separate the two signals — any hit on digikalas.online is high-priority; for raw TXT queries, filter out mail servers and confirm the querying process is not a mail/security service. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block digikalas.online and its subdomains at the resolver and isolate any endpoint that resolved it. 3) Hunt: correlate the client IP with UC1 C2 connections and UC2 scanner fan-out; if beaconing intervals appear, capture and decode the TXT responses for encoded commands and pivot on any new resolved IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "digikalas.online"
| extend Subdomain = tostring(split(RemoteUrl, ".digikalas.online")[0])
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, Subdomain, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Name endswith "digikalas.online" or QueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), QueryTypes = make_set(QueryTypeName), DistinctNames = dcount(Name), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by ClientIP, Name
| order by Queries desc

TuxBot/Akiru known ELF sample execution and drop (SHA256 pivot) AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution or file-write of the confirmed TuxBot v3 Evolution debug sample (SHA256 71dfbb17…), the x86_64 build with symbols submitted to VirusTotal on 2026-01-20. Article-specific single-hash pivot for the recovered bot binary, including its habit of hiding under a dot-prefixed filename. Rationale: Single confirmed IOC — the SHA256 71dfbb17…, the x86_64 debug build submitted to VirusTotal on 2026-01-20; an exact-hash match is unambiguous and the union covers both drop (FileWritten) and execution. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tuxbot-v3-evolution-shows-signs-of-llm.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or reverse-engineer detonating the known sample in a managed sandbox
  • EDR/AV telemetry from a quarantine or research VLAN where the sample is retained for study
  • Threat-intel platform hashing an archived copy during an automated enrichment sweep
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "malware-lab"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is not a sanctioned analysis VM; capture the full path (watch for a dot-prefixed hidden filename) and the parent process that dropped/launched it. 2) Contain: isolate the device, kill and quarantine the binary, and preserve it plus any persistence entries for forensics. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same SHA256 and for sibling GCC 14.2.0 production builds; pivot the host onto UC1 (C2 IPs/domain), UC2 (scanner fan-out) and UC3 (DGA/TXT DNS) to scope the infection stage.
let badhash = "71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d";
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 == badhash | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 == badhash | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 =~ "71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution

status: experimental

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

    - attack.initial-access

            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or SHA1 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or MD5 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or SHA1 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or MD5 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FacturaScripts upload endpoint: path-traversal sequence in multipart filename AIExploitation Medium
Hunts authenticated POSTs to FacturaScripts /api/3/uploadfiles or /api/3/attachedfiles where the request carries directory-traversal sequences (../, ..%2f, ..%5c) — the article's exact primitive for escaping MyFiles/ via the unsanitized getClientOriginalName() filename. Article-specific because legitimate FacturaScripts uploads never contain traversal syntax in the client filename. Rationale: Uses the article's named sinks (/api/3/uploadfiles, /api/3/attachedfiles) plus the ../ traversal signature that escapes MyFiles/. Note the traversal lives in the multipart Content-Disposition filename, not the URL — reliable only where a WAF/proxy inspects the body (CommonSecurityLog) or access logs capture request bodies; hence the companion file-write UCs. Defender XDR has no web-access-log table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/facturascripts/facturascripts/CVE-2026-27891/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vf3q-frmr-vrr9
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Burp/Acunetix) probing the FacturaScripts upload endpoints with traversal payloads
  • Authorized pentest engagement replaying this exact GHSA PoC
  • WAF false-positive matching literal '..' in a benign filename such as 'report..final.pdf'
  • Backup/sync tooling posting archive paths containing relative segments
Suppression filter
| where user!="" and NOT match(coalesce(http_user_agent,""),"(?i)(nessus|acunetix|nuclei|burp|zgrab|nmap)")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the alerting SourceIP — confirm the multipart filename contains ../ and identify the authenticated user/API token; check the HTTP response code (2xx = write likely succeeded). 2) Contain: revoke the offending API token/session and block the SourceIP at the WAF; snapshot Dinamic/Assets/ and node_modules/ for forensics before cleanup. 3) Hunt: pivot to the file-write and .htaccess-chain UCs on the same host/time window; enumerate any .php/.phtml/.htaccess written under Dinamic/Assets or node_modules and any subsequent GET to those paths returning PHP-executed output.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has_any ("uploadfiles","attachedfiles") or Message has_any ("uploadfiles","attachedfiles")
| where RequestURL has_any ("../","..%2f","..%5c","..\\") or Message has_any ("../","..%2f","..%5c","Path Traversal","directory traversal")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

FacturaScripts: PHP/.htaccess web-shell written into web-served Dinamic/Assets or node_modules AIInstallation High
Hunts the file-write outcome of the traversal: the web-server user creating a PHP-family file or an .htaccess override inside Dinamic/Assets/ or node_modules/ — the two directories the shipped htaccess-sample excludes from index.php rewriting, so Apache serves them directly. These paths should never receive attacker-controlled executable content in normal operation. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact web-served directories (Dinamic/Assets, node_modules) combined with the BLOCKED_EXTENSIONS-bypassing extensions (.htaccess plus php-family) and a web-server initiating process. A PHP or .htaccess file appearing in these asset dirs written by httpd/php/nginx is the traversal primitive landing on disk. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/facturascripts/facturascripts/CVE-2026-27891/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate FacturaScripts plugin install/update writing bundled PHP assets into Dinamic/
  • npm install/build repopulating node_modules with vendored .php or .htaccess sample files
  • Deployment/CI pipeline syncing application code into the web root
  • Developer manually copying a debugging PHP file into an assets folder
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","git.exe","msiexec.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","composer install","git checkout"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written file's content and hash (SHA256) — confirm it is PHP code or an AddType/AddHandler .htaccess rather than a benign asset; note the InitiatingProcess and account. 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the file, take the web app offline or drop a Deny-from-all rule over Dinamic/Assets, and rotate the web-server user's credentials/API tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate with the upload-endpoint UC for the originating request, look for a second dropped payload plus subsequent inbound GETs to the file path, and scan the whole web root for other newly-created php/htaccess files by the same process.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has "Dinamic" and FolderPath has "Assets") or FolderPath has "node_modules"
| extend Ext = tolower(tostring(split(FileName, ".")[-1]))
| where Ext in ("php","php3","php4","php5","php7","php8","pht","phtml","phps","phar","htaccess")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd.exe","apache.exe","apache2","httpd","php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","nginx.exe","caddy.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, Ext, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (TargetFilePath has "Dinamic" and TargetFilePath has "Assets") or TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| extend Ext = tolower(tostring(split(TargetFileName, ".")[-1]))
| where Ext in ("php","php3","php4","php5","php7","php8","pht","phtml","phps","phar","htaccess")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("httpd","apache","php","w3wp","nginx","caddy")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, Ext, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

FacturaScripts RCE chain: .htaccess handler-remap override plus payload drop in same asset dir AIExploitation High
Detects the article's Step-3 code-execution chain on the endpoint: an attacker-written .htaccess (remapping a benign extension to the PHP handler) landing in Dinamic/Assets or node_modules, immediately followed by a second file (the payload) in the same web-served directory. The .htaccess override in these Apache-direct-served folders is essentially never legitimate and is the linchpin that turns arbitrary write into RCE. Rationale: Chains the two writes the advisory's Step 3 spells out (upload .htaccess with AddType application/x-httpd-php, then upload x.png payload) into a single temporal correlation within a web-served asset dir — far higher fidelity than either write alone. The Falcon variant isolates the .htaccess override linchpin that uniquely enables the extension remap. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vf3q-frmr-vrr9
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application deployment that ships both an .htaccess and bundled assets into node_modules within the same window
  • FacturaScripts/plugin installer laying down a directory-level .htaccess alongside static files
  • CI artifact extraction writing an .htaccess and multiple assets together
  • Admin manually hardening an asset directory by dropping a Deny .htaccess next to existing files
Suppression filter

Response runbook
1) Triage: read the .htaccess contents (look for AddType/AddHandler/SetHandler mapping a non-PHP extension to php) and inspect the paired payload file for PHP code; capture the initiating web-server account. 2) Contain: delete both files, take the site offline or override the directory with Deny-from-all, and rotate the web-server user credentials and any upload-capable API tokens. 3) Hunt: review web logs for inbound GETs to the payload path (successful RCE trigger), check for outbound C2 from the web-server process, and sweep the entire document root for other .htaccess overrides written by the same process.

TidGi Desktop wiki worker spawning a command interpreter (TiddlyWiki startup-module RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE payload of GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv: after a malicious TiddlyWiki repo is imported, an auto-registered `module-type: startup` tiddler executes `require('child_process').execSync(...)` inside the TidGi Node.js wiki-worker thread, spawning a shell/LOLBin. A knowledge-management wiki app spawning cmd/powershell is anomalous and directly evidences exploitation. Rationale: Anchors on the exact exploit mechanics from the advisory (startup-module auto-exec calling require('child_process').execSync inside the TidGi wiki-worker) — a wiki app parenting cmd/powershell/LOLBins is high-fidelity. Cross-checked DeepWiki (worker-thread architecture runs in-process, so InitiatingProcess=TidGi.exe) and MITRE T1218.015. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv • https://deepwiki.com/tiddly-gittly/TidGi-Desktop/3.1-wiki-worker-and-nodejs-tiddlywiki • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/015/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059 T1218.015
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Wiki owner running their own PoC/security test of the advisory
  • A legitimately-installed TiddlyWiki plugin that intentionally shells out to a system tool
  • TidGi feature that opens an external file/URL via a helper that transits cmd.exe
  • Unrelated node.exe located in a folder path coincidentally containing the string 'TidGi'
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git ","--git-dir","rev-parse"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and TidGi's InitiatingProcessCommandLine; benign hits are usually git/backup helpers (excluded) — attacker payloads show execSync-style `cmd /c` with attacker commands. Identify the workspace folder and the most recently added tiddlers/*.js.tid file. 2) Contain: kill the TidGi and child process tree, isolate the host, and quarantine the imported wiki workspace directory to prevent re-boot re-execution. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for follow-on child processes, outbound connections from TidGi.exe, and any git.exe clone that delivered the repo; check other users who imported the same repo/URL.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("TidGi.exe","node.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "TidGi"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","calc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName endswith "\\TidGi.exe") or (ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" and ParentProcessName has "TidGi")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\curl.exe","\\calc.exe")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious startup-module tiddler (.js.tid) written into a TiddlyWiki tiddlers/ directory AIDelivery Low
Hunts the delivery artifact of GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv: import of a malicious repo drops a JavaScript module tiddler (title like `$:/plugins/poc/startup.js` → file `$__plugins__poc__startup.js.tid`) into the wiki's `tiddlers/` directory, which TidGi auto-loads and registers as an executable module at boot. Surfaces newly written `.js.tid` module tiddlers for content triage (check for `module-type: startup`). Rationale: Uses the advisory's concrete on-disk artifact (tiddler title `$:/plugins/poc/startup.js` serialised as a `.js.tid` file under `tiddlers/`) and the git-clone/TidGi/node writer of the import. File telemetry can't see `module-type: startup` content, so this is a triage hunt — pair with UC1 for confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv • https://deepwiki.com/tiddly-gittly/TidGi-Desktop/3-wiki-management-system
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.007 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate TiddlyWiki plugins commonly ship JavaScript module tiddlers as .js.tid files
  • User cloning/opening their own trusted wiki repository
  • TidGi updating or re-syncing bundled plugin tiddlers
  • Developer authoring a legitimate JS widget/macro tiddler in their workspace
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the flagged .js.tid file and check the tiddler header for `module-type: startup` (or `module-type: filteroperator`/`macro`) and `type: application/javascript` with a `text` body calling require/child_process/exec — benign plugin tiddlers rarely do. Note the workspace and whether a git clone immediately preceded the write. 2) Contain: if the body invokes shell/`child_process`, quarantine the workspace directory before TidGi next boots it and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (TidGi spawning a shell) on the same host/time; identify the source repo URL/folder and any other endpoints that imported it.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath

| where ActingProcessName has_any ("git.exe","TidGi.exe","node.exe")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] n8n-MCP cross-tenant workflow version read/enumeration via n8n_workflow_versions (CVE-2026-54052) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] n8n-MCP vulnerable multi-tenant config exposure (ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT without version-tool mitigation)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

n8n-MCP cross-tenant workflow version read/enumeration via n8n_workflow_versions (CVE-2026-54052) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts high fan-out use of the n8n-mcp `n8n_workflow_versions` tool in list/rollback mode within a single host/session, the read path an authenticated tenant abuses to pull other tenants' un-isolated version snapshots (which embed node credential references and auth headers). Article-specific because it keys on the exact vulnerable MCP tool name and its read modes rather than generic API abuse. Rationale: Keys on the exact vulnerable tool name `n8n_workflow_versions` and its read modes (list/rollback) confirmed in n8n-mcp docs, plus the tenant_id session parameter used by multi-tenant HTTP mode; fan-out threshold turns legitimate single-workflow use into an enumeration signal. Splunk uses a raw app-log search because n8n-mcp stdout has no native CIM datamodel home. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/czlonkowski/n8n-mcp • https://www.n8n-mcp.com/docs/workflow-management • https://docs.n8n.io/advanced-ai/mcp/mcp_tools_reference/
ATT&CKT1526 T1078 T1213
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate AI agent (Claude/Cursor/Windsurf) doing a bulk workflow audit or cleanup across many workflows in one session
  • Scheduled version-retention job iterating history to prune old snapshots
  • The one-time 2.56.1 upgrade migration touching all existing history
  • Platform admin performing a genuine multi-workflow restore/rollback
  • Monitoring/health-check that periodically lists versions
Suppression filter
| where ProcessName !has "migration" and Sample !has "retention" and Sample !has "scheduled-prune"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending host/session's raw n8n-mcp log lines; extract the acting tenant_id and the distinct workflow_ids/tenant_ids read — confirm whether the read tenant_id matches the owner tenant of each workflow. 2) Contain: if reads cross tenant boundaries, apply the advisory workaround immediately — set DISABLED_TOOLS=n8n_workflow_versions in the server env (Docker .env) and restart, or fail over each tenant to its own instance/DB; then upgrade to 2.56.1. 3) Hunt: for every foreign workflow_id touched, treat the embedded node credentials/auth headers as exposed — rotate them, and search the same logs for follow-on delete/prune/truncate (see companion UC).
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "n8n_workflow_versions"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ('"mode":"list"','"mode":"rollback"','mode=list','mode=rollback')
| extend WorkflowId = extract(@'(?i)workflow[_\-]?id["'':=\s]+([A-Za-z0-9]{6,})', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend TenantId  = extract(@'(?i)tenant[_\-]?id["'':=\s]+([A-Za-z0-9\-]{3,})', 1, SyslogMessage)
| summarize DistinctWorkflows = dcount(WorkflowId), Reads = count(), TenantIds = make_set(TenantId, 10), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, HostName, ProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctWorkflows > 20   // 20 = fan-out ceiling; a legit AI agent rarely reads >20 distinct workflow version histories per host/hour
| order by DistinctWorkflows desc
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype="n8n-mcp" OR sourcetype="n8n_mcp" OR source="*n8n-mcp*" OR source="*n8n_mcp*") "n8n_workflow_versions" ("\"mode\":\"list\"" OR "\"mode\":\"rollback\"" OR "mode=list" OR "mode=rollback")
| rex field=_raw "(?i)workflow[_\-]?id[\"':=\s]+(?<workflow_id>[A-Za-z0-9]{6,})"
| rex field=_raw "(?i)tenant[_\-]?id[\"':=\s]+(?<tenant_id>[A-Za-z0-9\-]{3,})"
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc(workflow_id) as distinct_workflows count as reads values(tenant_id) as tenant_ids min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen by host, _time
| where distinct_workflows > 20
| sort - distinct_workflows
n8n-MCP destructive workflow version backup deletion (delete/prune/truncate) — CVE-2026-54052 impact AIActions on Objectives Medium
Alerts on invocation of the n8n-mcp `n8n_workflow_versions` tool in delete/prune/truncate mode, the integrity/availability path an authenticated tenant abuses to destroy other tenants' un-isolated version backups. Article-specific: matches the exact tool name and its destructive modes rather than a generic file-delete pattern. Rationale: Matches the exact `n8n_workflow_versions` tool plus its three destructive modes (delete/prune/truncate confirmed in n8n-mcp docs) — the article explicitly states an authenticated tenant 'could delete or destroy other tenants' stored backups.' Destructive modes are rare enough to alert on; the query surfaces tenant_id/workflow_id so an analyst can immediately test cross-tenant ownership. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/czlonkowski/n8n-mcp • https://www.n8n-mcp.com/docs/workflow-management
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1485
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate retention maintenance using prune/truncate (normal housekeeping modes)
  • The 2.56.1 upgrade migration which intentionally clears previously un-scoped backups
  • Admin manually rolling back a bad version then deleting it
  • CI/CD redeploy pipeline that resets workflow version history
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "migration" and SyslogMessage !has "scheduled" and ProcessName !has "retention"
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the acting tenant_id and target workflow_id from the log line; verify whether the deleting tenant owns that workflow — a mismatch is a confirmed cross-tenant destruction. 2) Contain: disable the tool now (DISABLED_TOOLS=n8n_workflow_versions), restart the server, and restore affected version history from DB/offsite backup; upgrade to 2.56.1. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same tenant_id for prior list/rollback reads (recon before destruction) and treat any node credentials in the destroyed/read snapshots as compromised — rotate them.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "n8n_workflow_versions"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ('"mode":"delete"','"mode":"prune"','"mode":"truncate"','mode=delete','mode=prune','mode=truncate')
| extend WorkflowId = extract(@'(?i)workflow[_\-]?id["'':=\s]+([A-Za-z0-9]{6,})', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend TenantId  = extract(@'(?i)tenant[_\-]?id["'':=\s]+([A-Za-z0-9\-]{3,})', 1, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, TenantId, WorkflowId, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: n8n-MCP Destructive Workflow Version Backup Operation (CVE-2026-54052)
id: b3e1c7a2-4f8d-4a1e-9c3b-7d2e5f0a9c14
status: experimental
description: Detects invocation of the n8n-mcp n8n_workflow_versions tool in a destructive mode (delete/prune/truncate), the impact path of CVE-2026-54052 cross-tenant backup destruction in multi-tenant HTTP deployments.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-j6r7-6fhx-77wx
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/15
tags:
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1565.001
  - attack.t1485
logsource:
  product: n8n_mcp
  service: application
detection:
  selection_tool:
    message|contains: 'n8n_workflow_versions'
  selection_mode:
    message|contains:
      - '"mode":"delete"'
      - '"mode":"prune"'
      - '"mode":"truncate"'
  condition: selection_tool and selection_mode
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate version-retention pruning
  - The 2.56.1 upgrade migration that clears un-scoped backups
level: high
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype="n8n-mcp" OR sourcetype="n8n_mcp" OR source="*n8n-mcp*" OR source="*n8n_mcp*") "n8n_workflow_versions" ("\"mode\":\"delete\"" OR "\"mode\":\"prune\"" OR "\"mode\":\"truncate\"" OR "mode=delete" OR "mode=prune" OR "mode=truncate")
| rex field=_raw "(?i)workflow[_\-]?id[\"':=\s]+(?<workflow_id>[A-Za-z0-9]{6,})"
| rex field=_raw "(?i)tenant[_\-]?id[\"':=\s]+(?<tenant_id>[A-Za-z0-9\-]{3,})"
| table _time, host, source, tenant_id, workflow_id, _raw
| sort - _time
n8n-MCP vulnerable multi-tenant config exposure (ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT without version-tool mitigation) AIExploitation Low
Config-audit hunt: flags n8n-mcp instances running in multi-tenant HTTP mode (ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT=true) where the n8n_workflow_versions tool is NOT disabled and the build is at or below the vulnerable 2.56.0 — the exact preconditions for CVE-2026-54052 cross-tenant access. Article-specific because it keys on the named env vars, tool name, and fixed version from the advisory. Rationale: Uses the three concrete advisory facts — env var `ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT=true`, the `DISABLED_TOOLS=n8n_workflow_versions` mitigation string, and the fixed version boundary 2.56.0/2.56.1 — to surface exploitable instances before abuse. Low confidence because it assumes the server emits config/version in its startup logs; pair with a config-inventory check where available. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/czlonkowski/n8n-mcp • https://docs.n8n.io/advanced-ai/mcp/mcp_tools_reference/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Instance flagged multi-tenant but actually serving a single tenant (advisory says single-tenant HTTP is not affected)
  • Dev/test instance intentionally multi-tenant and not internet-exposed
  • Already-patched 2.56.1 host still echoing the env flag (version filter should exclude it, but startup log ordering may split the strings)
  • Instances where the version string isn't logged, causing an isnull() catch-all match
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "single-tenant" and HostName !has "dev" and HostName !has "test" and HostName !has "staging"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the flagged host is genuinely multi-tenant (>1 tenant/token served) and reachable by tenants — cross-check against the config-inventory/orchestration manifest. 2) Contain: for exposed vulnerable instances, apply a workaround now — set DISABLED_TOOLS=n8n_workflow_versions, or restrict the HTTP endpoint to trusted operators, then schedule the 2.56.1 upgrade (its migration isolates and clears un-scoped backups). 3) Hunt: on any instance that was vulnerable, replay the two companion detections (cross-tenant reads, destructive deletions) over the full exposure window to determine whether the gap was actually abused.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "n8n-mcp" or SyslogMessage has "n8n_mcp"
| where SyslogMessage has "ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT" and SyslogMessage has_any ("true","enabled")
| extend Version = extract(@'(?i)n8n[_\-]?mcp[^0-9]{0,20}v?(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend Mitigated = iif(SyslogMessage matches regex @'(?i)DISABLED_TOOLS\S*n8n_workflow_versions', true, false)
| extend Parts = split(Version, ".")
| extend VulnVersion = iif(isnotempty(Version) and (toint(Parts[0]) < 2 or (toint(Parts[0]) == 2 and (toint(Parts[1]) < 56 or (toint(Parts[1]) == 56 and toint(Parts[2]) <= 0)))), true, false)
| where Mitigated == false and (VulnVersion == true or isempty(Version))
| summarize Version = any(Version), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, HostName, ProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype="n8n-mcp" OR sourcetype="n8n_mcp" OR source="*n8n-mcp*" OR source="*n8n_mcp*") "ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT" ("true" OR "enabled")
| rex field=_raw "(?i)n8n[_\-]?mcp[^0-9]{0,20}v?(?<ver>\d+\.\d+\.\d+)"
| eval mitigated=if(match(_raw,"(?i)DISABLED_TOOLS\S*n8n_workflow_versions"),1,0)
| eval vuln_version=if(isnotnull(ver) AND (tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),0))<2 OR (tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),0))==2 AND (tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),1))<56 OR (tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),1))==56 AND tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),2))<=0)))),1,0)
| where mitigated=0 AND (vuln_version=1 OR isnull(ver))
| stats latest(ver) as version, latest(_raw) as sample, min(_time) as first_seen, max(_time) as last_seen by host, source
| sort - last_seen
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.

          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Anyquery process writing files to cron/webroot/SSH persistence paths (ATTACH DATABASE AFW) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-50006: Anyquery: Arbitrary File Write (AFW) which cou
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Reverse shell via cron/webshell payload dropped through Anyquery AFW (/dev/tcp)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Anyquery server mode bound to all interfaces (exposed unauthenticated MySQL port) AIDelivery High
Hunts for the Anyquery binary launched in `server` mode with a wildcard bind (0.0.0.0), which exposes the unauthenticated MySQL-compatible port abused in CVE-2026-50006 for ATTACH DATABASE arbitrary file write. Surfaces the attack-surface exposure before any exploitation occurs. Rationale: Uses the article's exact invocation `anyquery server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8070`; the combination of the named binary, the `server` subcommand and a wildcard bind is the precise exposure precondition for the CVE and is not a generic template. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx • https://github.com/julien040/anyquery/releases
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data/analytics team legitimately running Anyquery server on an internal, network-segmented host
  • Container image that binds 0.0.0.0 by convention but is only reachable inside a private overlay network
  • Developer running `anyquery server` in a local test/CI environment
  • Reverse-proxy fronted deployment where 0.0.0.0 bind is intentional but auth is enforced upstream
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Anyquery version (`anyquery --version`); anything < 0.4.5 is vulnerable. Check the bind address and whether the port is reachable from outside the host/subnet. 2) Contain: firewall the listener to localhost/trusted CIDRs or stop the service; upgrade to >= 0.4.5. 3) Hunt: on the same host review DeviceFileEvents for anyquery-initiated writes to /etc/cron.d, /var/www, /root/.ssh (see the AFW use case) and inbound connections from public IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "anyquery"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "server"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--host 0.0.0.0", "--host=0.0.0.0", "-h 0.0.0.0", "0.0.0.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has "anyquery"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "server"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound connection to Anyquery listener from a public IP AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for external (public-IP) network connections accepted by the Anyquery process, indicating an internet-reachable, unauthenticated MySQL-compatible endpoint is being reached by outside clients — the delivery vector for the CVE-2026-50006 ATTACH DATABASE write. Rationale: Ties the accepted inbound connection directly to the `anyquery` process (InitiatingProcess/ContextImageFileName) with a public remote peer, matching the article's 'unauthenticated attackers connecting to the MySQL-compatible server port'. Sentinel/Datadog left empty because inbound-accept events with process attribution are not present in the ASIM network or standard Datadog Linux schemas (explained per prompt guidance). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx
ATT&CKT1190 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate BI/reporting clients connecting to an intentionally public Anyquery endpoint
  • Cloud provider health-check probes hitting the exposed port
  • Internet-wide scanners (Shodan/Censys) touching the port without exploitation
  • VPN-exit / NAT gateway making internal client traffic appear as a single public IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: geolocate/reputation-check the RemoteIP and count distinct source IPs; a spray of unique public IPs suggests mass scanning. 2) Contain: restrict the listener to trusted source ranges and upgrade to Anyquery >= 0.4.5. 3) Hunt: for any RemoteIP of interest, pivot to DeviceFileEvents for anyquery writes to persistence paths and to DeviceProcessEvents for downstream cron/webshell reverse shells within the following minutes.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "anyquery"
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(LocalPort, 10), First = min(Timestamp), Last = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Connections desc

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "anyquery"
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(LocalPort, 10), First = min(TimeGenerated), Last = max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Connections desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/anyquery$/i
| ConnectionDirection=1
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, LocalPort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app=anyquery All_Traffic.direction=inbound by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app=anyquery All_Traffic.direction=inbound by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

Anyquery process writing files to cron/webroot/SSH persistence paths (ATTACH DATABASE AFW) AIInstallation High
Highest-fidelity detection for CVE-2026-50006: the Anyquery process itself creating files under cron directories, web roots, or SSH key paths. ATTACH DATABASE materialises a SQLite file at the attacker-chosen path, so a write by anyquery into /etc/cron.d, /var/spool/cron, /var/www, or /root/.ssh is a direct exploitation signal. Rationale: Combines the article's exact write targets (/etc/cron.d/pwn, /var/spool/cron/crontabs, /var/www/html/shell.php, /root/.ssh/authorized_keys) with the initiating process being anyquery — a database-federation tool that has no legitimate reason to write into cron/webroot/SSH. Datadog omitted because auditd file-target-path is not in the standard Datadog Linux schema. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx
ATT&CKT1190 T1053.003 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/restore tooling copying an Anyquery .db into /var/www or a home directory
  • Sysadmin manually redirecting Anyquery output to a file under an atypical path
  • Anyquery legitimately configured with its data directory pointed at a shared web-served folder
  • Config-management (Ansible/Puppet) running as the anyquery service account writing crontab entries
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "/var/www" and FileName endswith ".db" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--datadir")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the written file — a valid SQLite header (`SQLite format 3`) followed by cron/PHP/SSH-key text confirms the ATTACH DATABASE abuse. Note the target path and owning UID. 2) Contain: delete the malicious file, kill the anyquery process, isolate the host, and upgrade to >= 0.4.5. 3) Hunt: check cron execution and web/PHP process trees for the injected reverse-shell payload and review /root/.ssh/authorized_keys for attacker keys.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "anyquery"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/cron.hourly", "/etc/cron.daily", "/etc/crontab", "/var/www", "/root/.ssh") or FileName =~ "authorized_keys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "anyquery"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/cron.hourly", "/etc/cron.daily", "/etc/crontab", "/var/www", "/root/.ssh", "authorized_keys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
